name: Anyte
bio: Anyte of Tegea in Arcadia, an early third-century BC poet, wrote epitaphs, dedications and small scenes of country life, and was one of the women whom Meleager honoured in his Garland.
The epigrams here are the ones that Paton's first volume ascribes to her.

poems.title: Book VI, 123
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: Stand here, thou murderous spear, no longer drip from thy brazen barb the dismal blood of foes; but resting in the high marble house of Athene, announce the bravery of Cretan Echecratidas.

poems.title: Book VI, 153
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: The cauldron would hold an ox; the dedicator is Cleobotus, the son of Eriaspidas ; his city is spacious Tegea. The gift is made to Athene; the artist is Aristoteles of Cleitor, who bears the same name as his father.

poems.title: Book VI, 312
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: The children, billy-goat, have put purple reins on you and a muzzle on your bearded face, and they train you to race like a horse round the god’s temple that he may look on their childish joy.

poems.title: Book VII, 190
poems.author: Anyte
poems.note: Attribution doubtful in Paton (Anyte or Leonidas).
poems.text: For her locust, the nightingale of the fields, and her cicada that resteth on the trees one tomb hath little Myro made, shedding girlish tears; for inexorable Hades hath carried off her two pets.

poems.title: Book VII, 202: On a Cock
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: No longer, as of old, shalt thou awake early to rouse me from bed, flapping rapidly thy wings; for the spoiler stole secretly upon thee, as thou didst sleep, and slew thee, nipping thy throat swiftly with his claws.

poems.title: Book VII, 208
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: This tomb Damis built for his steadfast war-horse pierced through the breast by gory Ares. The black blood bubbled through his stubborn hide, and he drenched the earth in his sore death-pangs.

poems.title: Book VII, 215
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: No longer exulting in the sea that carries me, shall I lift up my neck as I rush from the depths; no longer shall I snort round the decorated bows of the ship, proud of her figure-head, my image. But the dark sea-water threw me up on the land and here I lie by this narrow (?) beach.

poems.title: Book VII, 486
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: Often on this her daughter’s tomb did Cleina call on her dear short-lived child in wailing tones, summoning back the soul of Philaenis, who ere her wedding passed across the pale stream of Acheron.

poems.title: Book VII, 490
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: I bewail virgin Antibia, eager to wed whom came many suitors to her father’s house, led by the report of her beauty and discretion; but destroying Fate in the case of all, sent their hopes rolling far away.

poems.title: Book VII, 492
poems.author: Anyte
poems.note: Attribution doubtful in Paton (Anyte of Mitylene?).
poems.text: We leave thee, Miletus, dear fatherland, refusing the lawless love of the impious Gauls, three maidens, thy citizens, whom the sword of the Celts forced to this fate. We brooked not the unholy union nor such a wedding, but we put ourselves in the wardship of Hades.;

poems.title: Book VII, 538
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: This man when alive was Manes, but now he is dead he is as great as great Darius.

poems.title: Book VII, 646
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: These were the last words that Erato spoke, throwing her arms round her dear father’s neck, her cheeks wet with fresh tears: “Father, I am thine no longer; I am gone, and sombre death casts already his black veil over my eyes.”

poems.title: Book VII, 649
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: Thy mother, Thersis, instead of a bridal chamber and solemn wedding rites, gave thee to stand on this thy marble tomb a maiden like to thee in stature and beauty, and even now thou art dead we may speak to thee.

poems.title: Book VII, 724
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: Thy valour, Proarchus, slew thee in the fight, and thou hast put in black mourning by thy death the house of thy father Phidias. But the stone above thee sings this good message, that thou didst fall fighting for thy dear fatherland.

poems.title: Book IX, 144
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: This is the place of Cypris, for it is sweet to her to look ever from the Jand on the bright deep, that she may make the voyages of sailors happy; and around the sea trembles, looking on her polished image.

poems.title: Book IX, 313
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: Sit here, quite shaded by the beautiful luxuriant foliage of the laurel, and draw sweet drink from the lovely spring, that thy limbs, panting with the labours of summer, may take rest beaten by the western breeze.

poems.title: Book IX, 314
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: Here stand I, Hermes, in the cross-roads by the wind-swept belt of trees near the grey beach, giving rest to weary travellers, and cold and stainless is the water that the fountain sheds.

poems.title: Book IX, 745
poems.author: Anyte
poems.text: Look on the horned goat of Bacchus, how haughtily with saucy eye he looks down on his flowing beard, exulting that often in the mountains the Naiad, caressing his cheeks, took those locks in her rosy hand.
